## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sakkapañha Sutta* (DN 21) is the twenty-first discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*, set at the Indasāla Cave near Rājagaha [Dhammika]. The narrative frame opens with Pañcasikha, a gandhabba and divine musician carrying a lute (*vīṇā*), who plays and sings a love song incorporating verses of devotion to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the arahants to secure an audience for Sakka, the ruler of the Tāvatiṃsa devas [SuttaCentral; Gnanarama 1998; Gorant; Jungnok Park 2012]. Sakka then questions the Buddha regarding the origin of social conflict, hostility, and suffering among beings who otherwise wish to live free of enmity [Gnanarama 1998; Kalmanson & Shields 2014]. The Buddha explains the causal sequence underlying conflict and attachment, tracing mental proliferation and concepts (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*) in relation to directed thought (*vitakka*), ideation, and desire (*chanda*) [Jungnok Park 2012; Hung 2010; Kalmanson & Shields 2014]. Sakka also declares that his ultimate destination will be rebirth in the Akaniṭṭha heaven [Tournier et al. 2018]. According to the Pali commentary (*Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*), during the delivery of this sutta Sakka died and was instantly reborn into the same divine body [Anālayo 2018].
The discourse exists in multiple recensions and traditions, though it was preserved outside the northern *Śakra-saṁyukta* collections [Bingenheimer 2011]. Its curated parallels include Chinese Āgama versions in the *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 14) and *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 134), individual Chinese translations such as T 15 (*Dìshì suǒwèn jīng*) and T 203.73, and Sanskrit fragments of the *Śakrapraśnasūtra* edited by Ernst Waldschmidt (SHT sutta 54, SF 139, SF 241), alongside thematic ties to Snp 3.6 (*Sabhiya Sutta*) [SuttaCentral; Nakamura 1980]. Cross-language alignments by DharmaNexus agree with these correspondences, showing significant textual overlaps with MĀ 134, DĀ 14, T 15, and the Sanskrit fragment SF 241 [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records extensive Pali-internal text reuse across 162 texts, including large shared passages with the *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta* (MN 114), the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), the *Navakanipāta* (AN 9), and the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [DharmaNexus].
